options.metric: Annual count of reported pedestrian casualties in Brooklyn crash reports, calculated by summing number_of_pedestrians_injured and number_of_pedestrians_killed.
options.denominator: No denominator; count of reported injured and killed pedestrians per calendar year.
options.reason: A total of injured and killed pedestrians gives a direct, easily understood measure of recorded pedestrian harm in the borough.
options.answer: Only partly answerable: the reported casualty count was 3,671 in 2013, reached a low of 1,798 in 2020, and stood at 2,874 in 2025.
options.interpretation: Only partly: this chart answers the reported-casualty-burden part by summing pedestrians injured and killed in Brooklyn police-reported crashes for each full calendar year; it shows 3,671 casualties in 2013, a low of 1,798 in 2020, and 2,874 in 2025. This is a defensible direct measure of recorded harm, but it cannot measure risk per pedestrian trip or person, so it cannot establish whether an individual pedestrian became safer. The check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 rows in 2013–2025 (30.9%) had missing, blank, unknown, or nonstandard borough labels and excluded them because Brooklyn could not be identified; no Brooklyn rows had either pedestrian outcome missing. The partial 2026 period, which ends June 11, was also excluded.

options.metric: Annual percentage of eligible Brooklyn crash reports with one or more pedestrians injured or killed; numerator counts reports with number_of_pedestrians_injured > 0 or number_of_pedestrians_killed > 0.
options.denominator: All police-reported Brooklyn crash rows in that calendar year with both pedestrian outcome fields nonmissing; these fields are complete for every included Brooklyn row, so this is all Brooklyn crash rows.
options.reason: The share of crash reports involving pedestrian casualties puts the event count in relation to the total number of Brooklyn crash reports that year.
options.answer: Only partly answerable: pedestrian-casualty crashes made up 7.44% of Brooklyn crash reports in 2013, 5.68% in 2017, and 11.38% in 2025.
options.interpretation: Only partly: this chart shows, for each full calendar year, the percentage of one-row-per-crash Brooklyn police reports that had one or more pedestrians injured or killed; the share was 7.44% in 2013, 5.68% in 2017, and 11.38% in 2025. This is a defensible measure of how often pedestrian casualties appeared among reported crashes, but it is not a pedestrian-trip or per-person risk measure and cannot establish whether walking became safer. The check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 rows in 2013–2025 (30.9%) had missing, blank, unknown, or nonstandard borough labels and excluded them; no Brooklyn rows had either pedestrian outcome missing, and partial 2026 (through June 11) was excluded. The denominator fell by 19,006 Brooklyn crash rows between 2019 (44,479) and 2020 (25,473), the largest neighboring-year change; across those years the share can change because of this denominator change and not the outcome, so compare it with that caution.

options.metric: Annual count of pedestrians reported killed in Brooklyn crash reports, calculated by summing number_of_pedestrians_killed.
options.denominator: No denominator; count of reported pedestrian deaths per calendar year.
options.reason: Pedestrian deaths isolate the most severe recorded outcome and are important to a local safety story even when annual counts are small.
options.answer: Only partly answerable: reported pedestrian deaths in Brooklyn numbered 30 in 2013, peaked at 46 in 2015, and numbered 39 in 2025.
options.interpretation: Only partly: this chart counts pedestrians reported killed in Brooklyn police-reported crashes by full calendar year; the count was 30 in 2013, peaked at 46 in 2015, and was 39 in 2025. Deaths are a defensible severe safety outcome, but this narrow count excludes nonfatal harm and cannot measure risk per pedestrian trip or person, so it cannot establish whether an individual pedestrian became safer. The check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 rows in 2013–2025 (30.9%) had missing, blank, unknown, or nonstandard borough labels and excluded them because Brooklyn could not be identified; no Brooklyn rows had a missing pedestrian-death field or grouping date. Partial 2026, which ends June 11, was excluded.
